intro: This branch shows how functions like sine or e to the x can be written as endless polynomials. That is how calculators actually compute them.

VI.10.01.what: A power series is a polynomial that never ends, with powers of x going on forever.

levels.a: Reads a power series written in sigma notation.
levels.b: Describes it as a polynomial that never ends.
levels.c: Adds up the first few terms to estimate a value.
levels.d: Identifies the center and the coefficients (the multiplying numbers).

VI.10.02.what: A power series only works for x values within a certain distance of its center, called the radius of convergence.

levels.a: Applies the ratio test to a power series.
levels.c: Handles series that work nowhere except the center, or everywhere.
levels.d: Handles series centered away from zero.

VI.10.03.what: Finding exactly which x values a power series works for, including checking the two edges.

levels.b: Decides whether each edge is included or not.
levels.c: Writes the full range of x values that work.
levels.d: Checks how the edges can change after differentiating the series.

VI.10.04.what: A Taylor polynomial is a simple polynomial built to imitate a complicated function near one point.

levels.a: Matches the function's value and derivatives at a point.
levels.b: Builds a Taylor polynomial of a given degree.
levels.c: Centers the polynomial at any chosen point.
levels.d: Graphs the polynomial against the function to see the fit.

VI.10.05.what: Writing e to the x as an endless polynomial, one of the most useful series in math.

levels.a: Derives the series for e to the x.
levels.b: Uses it to approximate the number e.
levels.c: Substitutes to get new series, like e to the minus x squared.
levels.d: Shows the series works for every value of x.

VI.10.06.what: Writing sine and cosine as endless polynomials.

levels.a: Derives the series for sine and cosine.
levels.b: Notices sine uses only odd powers and cosine only even powers.
levels.c: Uses the series to approximate a value.
levels.d: Uses small-angle shortcuts, like sine of x being nearly x.

VI.10.07.what: Series for one over one minus x, built from repeated multiplication, and for related functions like the logarithm.

levels.a: Writes the repeated-ratio (geometric) series as a power series.
levels.b: Integrates it to get the series for the logarithm.
levels.c: Substitutes to get the series for arctangent.
levels.d: Shows these series work only for x between minus one and one.

VI.10.08.what: Making new series quickly from known ones instead of starting from scratch.

levels.a: Substitutes an expression for x in a known series.
levels.b: Multiplies a series by a power of x.
levels.d: Finds a particular coefficient quickly using these tricks.

VI.10.09.what: Differentiating and integrating series one term at a time, like ordinary polynomials.

levels.a: Differentiates or integrates a series term by term.
levels.b: Knows the radius of convergence stays the same.
levels.c: Finds the total of a series by differentiating a known one.
levels.d: Integrates a series to build a new one.

VI.10.10.what: Multiplying and dividing series to find the first few terms of a new series.

levels.a: Finds the first few terms of a product of two series.
levels.b: Divides the sine series by the cosine series to get tangent.
levels.c: Keeps track of which powers are needed.

VI.10.11.what: A guarantee on how far off a Taylor polynomial's estimate can be.

levels.b: Finds the largest size of the next derivative on the range.
levels.c: Uses the formula to bound the error.
levels.d: Chooses how many terms are needed for a desired accuracy.

VI.10.12.what: For alternating series, the error from stopping early is no bigger than the first term left out.

levels.a: Uses the next term as a bound on the error.
levels.c: Decides whether the estimate is too high or too low.
levels.d: Compares this with the general error bound.

VI.10.13.what: Expanding one plus x raised to any power, even a fraction or negative number, as an endless series.

levels.a: Writes the series for one plus x to any power.
levels.c: Approximates square roots of numbers close to one.
levels.d: Shows the series works only for x between minus one and one.

VI.10.14.what: Euler's formula links exponentials to sine and cosine using imaginary numbers. It leads to a famous equation joining five key numbers.

levels.a: Derives e to the i theta by substituting into the exponential series.
levels.b: Shows it equals cosine theta plus i times sine theta.
levels.c: Derives e to the i pi plus one equals zero.
levels.d: Links the formula to the polar form of imaginary numbers.

VI.10.15.what: Using series to handle integrals that have no ordinary formula, such as the one behind the bell curve.

levels.a: Recognizes integrals with no standard formula answer.
levels.b: Integrates the function's series term by term.
levels.c: Approximates the integral's value from a few terms.
levels.d: Bounds the error of the approximation.

VI.10.16.what: Finding tricky limits by replacing functions with their series and seeing which terms matter.

levels.a: Replaces each function in the limit with its series.
levels.b: Cancels the leading terms that cause trouble.
levels.c: Finds the limit from what remains.
levels.d: Compares this method with L'Hôpital's rule.
